text.hook:
"`clear()` gives the memory back."
It does not. The capacity stays.

The std::vector mental model, plus 6 myths that fail interviews. Swipe ➜ and save it.
text.body:
Inside:
1. Three pointers, one heap block
2. Growth factors by library
3. reserve vs resize
4. What reallocation does, in order
5. Six myths, busted (slides 8-9)

Which myth did you believe? Comment the slide number.

slides.lead: Three pointers, a growth factor, and the rules that decide when your pointers die.

slides.title: Three pointers, one heap block
slides.takeaway: Slots in `[end, end_of_storage)` are raw memory. Reading or writing them is UB, even though they are allocated.

slides.title: Growth on `push_back`
slides.takeaway: Geometric growth makes `push_back` amortized O(1). The libstdc++ row is verified with GCC 11.

slides.title: Who creates elements?
slides.takeaway: `reserve` changes capacity only. `resize` changes the size, and grows capacity when needed.

slides.title: `emplace_back` at full capacity
steps: Allocate a new block, larger by the growth factor
Construct the **new element first**, at index `size()`
Relocate the old elements with `move_if_noexcept`, destroy them, free the old block: every old pointer is now invalid
That order is why `v.push_back(v[0])` is safe: the argument lives until the old block is freed

slides.title: Where `emplace_back` wins
slides.takeaway: `emplace_back` only saves work when you pass constructor arguments.

slides.lead: It stores bits. `operator[]` returns a proxy object, not `bool&`: `&vb[0]` is not a `bool*`, there is no `data()`, and writes to different elements can race.

items.truth: Only when you pass constructor arguments. `emplace_back(t)` is the same copy.

items.myth: "`push_back` at full capacity might not reallocate."
items.truth: It must: capacity is the storage the vector holds.

items.myth: "Reallocation moves the old elements first, then builds the new one."
items.truth: libstdc++ builds the new element first. That is why `push_back(v[0])` works.
It is UB. Only `at()` checks and throws `out_of_range`.
Capacity stays. Use `shrink_to_fit` (a request) or swap with an empty vector.
A copy allocates for the elements only. A move keeps the block.

slides.lead: Save this. Follow for a C++ interview puzzle every day.

`reserve(n)` first, so the loop never reallocates.
Then fill by index.
Approved in review.

text.body: A rotate by index that looks correct line by line.

slides.title: What does it print?

bullets: `reserve(n)` allocates room for `n` ints but creates no elements: `size()` stays 0.
`r[i]` writes raw memory inside the block: UB, no check, no exception.
`r` still has `begin == end`, so the loop prints nothing.

slides.title: Size the vector before indexing
slides.tip: Appending in order instead? Then `reserve(n)` plus `push_back` is the right pair.

text.hook:
`v(10)`, `v{10}`, `v(10, 5)`, `v{10, 5}`.
Then `emplace_back(10)` vs `push_back({10})`.
Six sizes.

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: Every C++ developer has written one of these by accident.

slides.title: What does it print?

bullets: Parentheses pick the size constructors: `(10)` ten zeros, `(10, 5)` ten fives.
Braces pick the `initializer_list` constructor when viable: `{10}` one element, `{10, 5}` two.

slides.title: Parentheses for counts, braces for values

Then `flags[0] = true;`.

text.body: With `std::vector<int>` this is boring. This one is a `vector<bool>`.

slides.title: What does it print?

bullets: `auto first` is that proxy: it keeps referring to bit 0 and reads the later write: `1`.
`bool copy` converts the proxy to a value at that moment: `0`.

slides.title: Spell out `bool` when you want a value
slides.tip: `&flags[0]` is not a `bool*` and there is no `data()`. Need real bools? `std::vector<char>`.
slides.takeaway: `vector<bool>` stores bits and hands out proxies.

Remove every 2 from the vector with `std::remove`.
Then print the size.

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: The algorithm's name promises more than it can do.

slides.title: What does it print?

slides.verdict_sub: Tail values are unspecified: `2 5` is libstdc++ / GCC 11, x86-64
bullets: `std::remove` shifts the kept elements (`1 3 5`) to the front and returns the new logical end: index 3.
It cannot change the size: algorithms see iterators, not the container.
The tail holds valid but unspecified values.

slides.title: `remove` reorders, `erase` shrinks
slides.takeaway: `std::remove` never changes `size()`. Pair it with `erase`, or use C++20 `std::erase`.
